stature.source: typical: FEIS, usually 20-24 m, lowered a little for subcanopy trees under redwood in Marin; tall: an estimate; record: FEIS, the champion near Ophir, Oregon, 144 ft (43.9 m); read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values, no photographs measured: FEIS, subcanopy trees have narrow crowns and shaded trunks self-prune, often clear for 9-24 m; open-grown trees are broad and rounded (the young class)

young.note: a sprout clump or young tree, rounded and leafy low down, often several stems from one burl

veteran.note: a tall old tree with two or three stems from a burl, a long clear trunk and a ragged rounded top in the gaps of the redwood canopy

description: An evergreen relative of the oaks that grows in the redwood and mixed evergreen forest, slim and tall under the conifers and round-headed in the open. Its thick, toothed leaves are woolly and buff underneath when young, and it bears big acorns in shaggy cups.

season_notes.winter: Leathery leaves hold their olive green in the rain; last fall's acorns lie under the trees.
season_notes.spring: New shoots come out felted and pale buff, the crown looks frosted.
season_notes.summer: Erect cream catkins stand over the crown with a heavy smell.
season_notes.fall: Large acorns in bristly cups fall, after two summers on the tree.

range.where: redwood and mixed evergreen forest from southwest Oregon south through the Coast Ranges; Marin and the Santa Cruz Mountains, rarely on the Peninsula north of them

notes: Grown from canyon live oak (same family, evergreen, leathery toothed leaves) but made narrower and taller with a longer leader and a clear bole, as FEIS describes subcanopy trees; the broad open-grown form is the young class. The colour is paler and more olive than canyon live oak, and the spring crown is pale with felted new shoots (FEIS: first-year leaves densely hairy, older ones nearly hairless with a waxy top); the palette's pale entries stand for the woolly undersides that show when the wind turns the leaves. Its flowers are erect catkins, drawn as cream candles in summer. Cannot express: the burl and its dense ring of sprouts after fire (FEIS: up to about 100 sprouts on a large burl), and the sudden oak death that kills many tanoaks today (an introduced pathogen; a world without people might not have it, so the snag share is kept low). Dusky-footed woodrats and northern flying squirrels depend on its mast (FEIS) but are not in the animal library. FEIS's elevation figure is inconsistent (7,500 ft vs 1,500 m); 1,500 m is used.
